I need to write a JUnit 4 test class for TarArchiveInputStream with broad branch coverage, restricted to only hamcrest-core, junit-4.11, and xz-1.5 -- so no Mockito or other helper libraries, meaning I'll need to construct actual tar files in-memory for the tests.

I'm mapping out the key methods to cover: constructors, available(), skip(), reset(), the many branches in getNextTarEntry() (EOF, GNU long link/name, PAX headers, GNU sparse), skipRecordPadding(), getLongNameData(), getRecord(), isEOFRecord(), readRecord(), PAX header parsing and application, GNU sparse handling, the read() method's various exit conditions, canReadEntryData, and entry accessor/mutator methods plus consumeRem().

Now I'm reasoning through the static matches() method's branches for header length and magic string detection (POSIX, GNU, ANT), then thinking about whether I can rely on TarArchiveEntry and other commons-compress classes being compiled and available on the classpath since they're part of the same source tree as the class under test.

I'm planning to use TarArchiveOutputStream to construct valid tar byte streams for positive test cases, and build malformed byte arrays manually for negative-path tests. Writing helper method for building simple tar archives...

I'll assume TarArchiveOutputStream is available from commons-compress and reliable enough to use as a test helper. Now I'm planning out test cases covering different constructor variants—default, with encoding, with block size, and combinations thereof—verifying record size defaults and configuration.

For the available() tests, I need to check normal behavior after reading an entry, plus a boundary case where entrySize minus entryOffset exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE; since there's no public setter for entrySize, I'll use reflection to directly manipulate that private field for testing this edge case. I'm also planning skip() tests, covering both a normal in-entry skip and a skip that goes beyond the available bytes.

For reset(), I just need to confirm it's a no-op with no exception thrown. For getNextTarEntry(), I'm testing the EOF path where an empty underlying stream immediately triggers hasHitEOF, causing both the first and subsequent calls to return null, plus a malformed header case where garbage bytes cause the TarArchiveEntry constructor to throw an exception.

I'm hesitant to assume exactly how TarArchiveEntry validates its header bytes without seeing its source, so I want to avoid guessing at internal parsing behavior that isn't actually confirmed by the provided code.

Given the uncertainty, I'll avoid speculative exception-throwing assertions for malformed headers since I can't verify actual TarArchiveEntry behavior without its source, and instead focus on tests I can confidently validate.

Given the ambiguity around whether that exception behavior is guaranteed by the source, I'll drop the malformed-header test and instead focus only on well-defined paths in TarArchiveInputStream, like the null header case. Next I want to test the scenario where getNextTarEntry is called while currEntry is already set, building a tar with two entries to verify it advances correctly.

For long GNU names, I recall TarArchiveOutputStream supports setLongFileMode with LONGFILE_GNU, so I'll use that to write an entry with a name over 100 characters and confirm the long name gets parsed correctly. For Pax headers, I'll need to manually construct an entry with a 'x' typeflag since the simple API may not directly expose Pax header writing.

I'll rely on TarArchiveOutputStream's public putArchiveEntry/write/closeArchiveEntry methods to build valid tar content for positive tests, and craft raw bytes directly for negative/malformed cases like EOF markers or incomplete records. For the pax header test, I'm considering whether that historical version of commons-compress even writes PAX headers automatically, since manually constructing one would be complex.

Since PAX-triggering config is version-dependent and risky to guess, I'll instead construct a raw header block by hand using the well-known USTAR/GNU tar field layout — since that layout is a standard specification the library implements, not something I'm guessing about the library's internal behavior, it should be safe to hardcode.

Actually, I realize a simpler and safer approach: since parsePaxHeaders is package-private, I can put my test in the same package and call it directly, bypassing the need to construct full tar entries or guess integration behavior. applyPaxHeadersToCurrentEntry and paxHeaders() are private though, so those remain inaccessible even from the same package.

Placing the test in `org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.tar` also unlocks other protected/package-private members like readRecord, isEOFRecord, getLongNameData, setCurrentEntry, and isAtEOF/setAtEOF, which opens up a lot of white-box testing opportunities without needing valid tar files for every branch. I'm now sketching direct unit tests on these isolated methods, starting with isEOFRecord for null and other edge-case inputs.

Testing readRecord with buffers shorter and exactly equal to the record size, then working through parsePaxHeaders with carefully constructed minimal PAX header records where the length prefix must exactly match the total record length.

Continuing the trace, after the space it reads the keyword "a" up to the "=", then computes the remaining bytes as len minus what's been read so far, leaving exactly 1 byte for the value which turns out to just be the trailing newline. That means the value ends up empty, so "a" maps to an empty string in headers before the loop moves to the next entry.

Now I want to test a case with a real value, like key "path" set to "foo", where the tricky part is that the header's length prefix must account for its own digit count -- so I need to solve for L iteratively since L appears inside the string whose length it describes.

Trying L=15 with "15 path=foo\n", I recount the actual characters and get only 12, not 15, so my guess was wrong and I need to redo the calculation with L=12 instead.

Verifying "12 path=foo\n": digits contribute 2, space 1, "path=foo" 8, newline 1, totaling exactly 12 -- that checks out this time. Tracing through the parser confirms it reads the length correctly, extracts "path" as the keyword, then reads the remaining 4 bytes "foo\n" as the value, matching the expected size.

Now I'm wondering whether to build a fuller integration test with an actual pax extended header tar entry (typeflag 'x') followed by a normal entry to exercise the full getNextTarEntry() pax-detection path, but that requires knowing TarConstants field offsets that aren't given in the source, which makes constructing a valid header tricky.

Writing tar header builder...

I also want to cover getRecord() branches like hasHitEOF and consumeRemainderOfLastBlock, but these are private and only reachable through getNextTarEntry, requiring a stream with two full zero blocks sized to the default block/record constants -- manageable but requiring a sizable buffer allocation.

To simplify, I'll use a custom constructor with matching block and record sizes so bytesReadOfLastBlock math is straightforward, testing the zero-skip branch first, then adjusting blockSize larger than recordSize to trigger the positive skip branch.

Actually the try block always attempts readRecord() regardless of markSupported, so shouldReset gets computed either way. Since ByteArrayInputStream actually supports mark/reset, the marked=true path gets exercised too, giving good coverage of both branches without throwing exceptions.

Let me plan the byte layout for a getNextTarEntry EOF test using blockSize=1024 and recordSize=512 via the constructor that accepts both. If the input is exactly one all-zero 512-byte record and nothing else, readRecord() reads exactly 512 bytes and returns it (not null), isEOFRecord detects all zeros so hasHitEOF becomes true, and since headerBuf isn't null it proceeds to tryToConsumeSecondEOFRecord.

That call marks the stream, but since the input is fully consumed the second readRecord returns null (zero bytes read, not matching recordSize), so isEOFRecord(null) is true and shouldReset is false, meaning no reset happens regardless of the mark. Then consumeRemainderOfLastBlock computes bytesReadOfLastBlock as 512 mod 1024 = 512, so it tries to skip the remaining 512 bytes, but the stream is already empty so skip just returns 0 with no exception. The net result is that getNextTarEntry() returns null cleanly, with currEntry set to null.

Now I need to test the opposite branch of tryToConsumeSecondEOFRecord where shouldReset is true — meaning the first record is all zeros (marking EOF) but the second record contains real, non-zero data, which should trigger the parser to reset the stream and treat that second record as an actual entry rather than confirming end-of-archive. I'm constructing a test input with a 512-byte all-zero record followed by a 512-byte non-zero record to verify this reset behavior: the first read hits EOF detection, marks the position, reads the second record, finds it's not an EOF record, sets shouldReset to true, and since it was marked, calls pushedBackBytes and resets the stream.

Given the internal state complexities around bytesRead and skip logic after reset, I'll settle for asserting that no exception is thrown and the final return value is null, since headerBuf gets unconditionally nulled regardless of these internal details, making this a safe, verifiable assertion from the source.

I also want to test isEOFRecord() directly for null input, an all-zero record, and a non-zero record, plus readRecord() with insufficient and exact-size byte arrays. For testing skip(long), I'm considering setting up a full round trip using TarArchiveOutputStream to create a valid tar with a known entry.

For available() and read(), I'm thinking through edge cases like entrySize exceeding Integer.MAX_VALUE and the scenario where currEntry is null but entryOffset is less than entrySize -- I realize this branch isn't reachable through normal API usage, so I'll use reflection to force those private fields for coverage purposes.

I still need to test partial reads within a normal entry, and simulate a corrupted stream where the underlying read hits EOF mid-entry to verify hasHitEOF gets set correctly. Testing sparse entries is tricky since I'm not sure of the exact API for marking a TarArchiveEntry as GNU sparse, so I'll skip that branch and focus on the two clearly testable cases: non-TarArchiveEntry returning false, and a typical non-sparse entry returning true. For the matches() static method, testing the true branches would require exact magic byte values from TarConstants that I don't have access to, so I'll need to work around that limitation too.

This avoids hardcoding literal magic strings myself, letting the library define its own format—that's a robust test without guesswork. I'll also verify the "length too short" branch returns false for a zero-length array, since that's guaranteed by pure logic without needing assumptions. And I want to test a buffer of correct length but all-zero bytes, which should also return false since zero bytes don't correspond to any of the valid magic strings.

For GNU longname support, I'll use setLongFileMode with LONGFILE_GNU, which I believe existed on TarArchiveOutputStream in this commons-compress version, flagging it as an assumption.
